<margin>Commentary of Su <note>referring to Su Shi, 1037 to 1101</note></margin>Those who do not know the <term>Tao</term> <gloss>the Way</gloss> but strive for learning will find that what they hear and see increases daily. Yet, without a way to unify this knowledge, it inevitably becomes a burden. Confucius said: "To hear much, select what is good and follow it; to see much and remember it—this is the second level of knowledge." <note>A reference to the Analects 7.28, suggesting that empirical accumulation is inferior to intuitive realization.</note> If one day you know the Way, you will look back on the false and the artificial; nothing there is not delusional. To remove delusion and return to your true nature is what is called "decreasing." Confucius said to <term>Zigong</term> <gloss>a prominent disciple</gloss>: "Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all?" Zigong replied, "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said, "No, I unify it all with one principle." <note>Analects 15.3</note> Forgetting the mind to purely return to nature is called "decreasing." Once delusion no longer exists, and one reaches the point of forgetting even this mind to purely return to nature with nothing remaining, then one can depart from "acting" without losing the state of <term>wu-wei</term> <gloss>non-action or effortless action</gloss>. All people have desires to "take" the world through logic and affairs. Thus, they create tasks and seek outcomes, but this is visible to others, and the world dislikes it; therefore, it is difficult and cannot be achieved. The Sage practices non-action and thus his mind is free of affairs. This is visible to others, and the world is at peace with it. Although he does not "take" the world or its affairs, the world and its affairs follow and find peace through him.

<margin>Commentary of Lü <note>likely Lü Huiqing, 1032 to 1111</note></margin>One who pursues learning is one who has not yet heard the Way. To seek it without hearing it, one must be broad, thus it is said "one increases daily." One who pursues the Way is one who has already heard the Way. Having heard it and practicing it, one must simply practice non-action, thus it is said "one decreases daily." "Decreasing and further decreasing" means one has not yet escaped the state of having action. One must decrease even that which does the decreasing. Only then does one reach non-action. Non-action means a state of being still and unmoving. "Nothing left undone" means that when stimulated, one responds and thus penetrates all the causes of the world. Moving from non-action to reaching the ultimate non-action is called the Constant. Learning without worry is called divine. The direction of the divine is the Way. Who but the most divine can participate in this? From this perspective, taking the world is always done through non-action. As for those who use "action," it is clear they are not sufficient to take the world.

<column-break/>

<margin>Commentary of Huang Maocai <note>a Southern Song dynasty scholar</note></margin>Only when there is nothing one does not know can one speak of "learning," therefore learning desires daily increase. Only when there is nothing one does not "do" can one speak of the Way, therefore the Way desires daily decrease. However, increase can be sought through progress, while decrease is sometimes difficult to achieve through force. Only the most enlightened can suddenly drop all attachments to reach the realm of non-action. Thus, they can do everything, and their application is inexhaustible; they move through the world with ample room and ease.

<margin>Commentary of Xizhai <note>the pen name of Li Kan, 1245 to 1320</note></margin>Pursuing learning is the means to seek knowledge, hence it increases daily. Pursuing the Way is the means to remove delusion, hence it decreases daily. If knowledge is not ultimate, then the decrease will not be complete. Therefore, "daily increase" serves as the foundation for "daily decrease." If one decreases and further decreases until delusion is gone and truth is complete, then there is non-action. Upon reaching non-action, even when there is action, it has never not been "non-action." This is no longer easily discussed in terms of "increase" or "decrease." When non-action reaches its peak, though the world is vast and manifold, it is unified by one principle. If one tries to manage the world by creating affairs, even a single thing will be entangled and mistaken; how much more so with the many things of the world?

The Sage has no constant <term>xin</term> <gloss>heart-mind</gloss>; he takes the heart-mind of the people as his own. To those who are good, I am good; to those who are not good, I am also good. Thus <term>Te</term> <gloss>Virtue/Inner Power</gloss> is goodness. To those who are faithful, I am faithful; to those who are not faithful, I am also faithful. Thus Virtue is faithfulness. The Sage in the world is cautious <note>original: 惛惛 (hun-hun), suggesting a state of being dim or undifferentiated</note> and unifies his heart for the sake of the world. The people all focus their ears and eyes upon him; the Sage <note>The text likely continues to say "treats them all as children."</note>

<page-num>Twenty-two</page-num>

<summary>This page contains various scholarly commentaries on Chapters 48 and 49 of the Tao Te Ching, emphasizing that spiritual progress requires "decreasing" or shedding worldly knowledge and delusions to reach the state of non-action. The main text describes the Sage as a selfless figure who adopts the people's perspective and maintains virtue regardless of others' behavior.</summary>
<keywords>Laozi, Tao Te Ching, non-action, Wu-wei, daily decrease, heart-mind, Sage, virtue, Su Shi, Lü Huiqing, Huang Maocai, Li Kan</keywords>
